The Opus research agent's answer (11:33 CST, sourced from code.claude.com and platform.claude.com): keep Claude Code. Do not build your own harness. If you build anything, build only the layer that passes messages between sessions, on top of Claude Code.

Why:
1. Talk across machines needs a claude.ai sign-in. Remote Control, cross-session messages and cloud sessions do not work on an API key (code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control, /cross-session-messaging). An SDK or API harness loses exactly what you want, and you would build the transport and hosting yourself.
2. The Agent SDK runs the same claude CLI underneath (/agent-sdk/overview). It loads the same hooks and skills, so it keeps the Windows gaps and the auto-mode refusals. A raw API harness drops all 36 of your hook registrations, plus compaction, caching, permissions and worktrees, and you rebuild them.
3. Cost: your plan is a flat fee. The API charges per token: Opus 5.5 $4 in, $20 out per million tokens (platform.claude.com pricing). Your volume is unmeasured.

Why the app feels poor (documented): the old terminal view flickers and grows in memory, and full-screen mode fixes it but is a preview; Windows Terminal leaves stale text. Remote Control needs the local process running, and server mode drops after about 10 min without network. A cloud session cannot reply to another machine with SendMessage; WSL and native Windows cannot reach each other. The cause is where sessions run and how they connect, not the app's shell; your own harness would face the same network problems. Electron itself is unverified (no official source).

Your Windows fcntl gap is in our code, not the harness: hooks/ci_wake.py:196 and janitor/agent_end_reap.py:79 (sent to the windows-local-lint lane).

Cheapest test: item 273, a 5-message check across Mac, PC and cloud.
